pages.title: Africa's importance for India; Gandhi and Nehru
pages.summary: Africa has six of the fastest-growing economies in sub-Saharan Africa and draws China, USA, Britain, France, Japan and Russia. Its importance for India lies in trade, investment, energy, food and maritime security, plus terrorism and piracy risks, and Gandhi wanted a commerce of ideas and services while Nehru held India's independence incomplete without Africa's liberation.

pages.title: Leaders' visions; first two phases of relations
pages.summary: Manmohan Singh called the partnership a two-way street, and Modi said it goes beyond strategy and is not transactional, citing vasudhaiva kutumbakam and ubuntu. India backed African liberation till the 1960s, then neglected Africa from the 1970s to 90s after African attitudes on the 1962 war and violence against Indians.

pages.title: Renewed engagement since 1990s; 2008 summit
pages.summary: From the 1990s Africa gained importance as democracy, business climate and integration improved, with Indian IT and pharmaceutical firms leading and the government responding late. India held its first India-Africa summit in 2008, eight years behind China's 2000 forum, and all 54 countries attended in 2015.

pages.title: 2016 visits and initiatives; China competition begins
pages.summary: Heads of State or Government of 40 countries attended the 2015 summit, and in 2016 the President, Vice President and PM Modi visited African states important for India's Indian Ocean maritime focus. Initiatives include ITEC, Team 9 and the Pan-African e-network, with a capacity-building approach, and the first challenge listed is competition from China.

pages.title: China competition, Africa policy and diaspora
pages.summary: India-Africa trade is $72 bn against $200 bn for China-Africa, but Manmohan Singh sees space for both and India's strengths are IT, pharmaceuticals and capacity building. The notes add that India lacks a declared Africa policy and, per Siddharth Varadarajan, needs a stronger diplomatic presence and diaspora outreach beyond the elite.

pages.title: Corporate redlines, Sachdev's advice, racial violence
pages.summary: The government should set redlines for private firms accused of land grabbing, enforce corporate social responsibility and create special purpose vehicles for fast delivery. Mahesh Sachdev urges a SWOT analysis and making Africans stakeholders, and the notes call for redress of racial violence against Africans in India and for African studies.

pages.title: Gandhian guide for Africa; Latin America opens
pages.summary: India must understand African culture and treat the relationship as a genuine two-way street guided by Gandhi, and Modi's vision is a partnership that helps people make choices. Latin America is the last frontier of India's foreign policy, where psychology rather than geography is the barrier, China is overwhelmingly present and India lacks consulates in all countries.

pages.title: Latin America history; resentment against China
pages.summary: Except Cuba, India had poor relations with Latin America because of the region's instability, US domination and India's inward-looking economy. After the Cold War stability and growth came, Indian private firms led, and an Inter-American Development Bank report in 2010 called India Latin America's next big thing amid resentment of Chinese practices.

pages.title: Latin America opportunity, connectivity and visits
pages.summary: Latin America seeks India as an alternative to China, offering a 600 mn population, per capita income of $11,000 and oil, gas and mineral reserves, but connectivity is the biggest challenge. India has a PTA only with Chile and Mercosur, high-level visits are few, and the notes urge FTAs, shipping incentives and mutual area studies.

pages.title: Latin America challenges, CELAC and trade figures
pages.summary: Geography, distance, diversity and lack of historical and cultural links complicate ties, though Bollywood is an emerging area of cooperation. After CELAC's 2012 outreach summit in New Delhi, India got a programme of action, a special office and Pacific Alliance observer status, with trade of $100 bn in 2017 against China's $264 bn.

flashcards.front: Why is Africa important for India?
flashcards.back: Africa matters for trade, investment, energy security, food security and the security of India's maritime trade. It is also becoming a hub of Islamic fundamentalism, transnational terrorism, piracy and organised crime.

flashcards.front: What were Gandhi's and Nehru's views on India's approach to Africa?
flashcards.back: Gandhi said India and Africa should have a commerce of ideas and services, not of raw materials like imperialist powers. Nehru held that India's independence remained incomplete without the liberation of Africa.

flashcards.front: What are the three phases of India-Africa relations in the notes?
flashcards.back: Till the 1960s India actively supported African liberation. From the 1970s to 90s it neglected Africa after African attitudes on the 1962 war and violence against Indians, and from the 1990s engagement revived, led by the private sector.

flashcards.front: When was the first India-Africa summit held and how did it compare with China?
flashcards.back: India's first India-Africa summit was in 2008, eight years behind China, which began its China-Africa cooperation forum in 2000. At the 2015 summit all 54 African countries took part, 40 of them at head of state or government level.

flashcards.front: How do India-Africa and China-Africa trade compare, and what advice is given on the rivalry?
flashcards.back: India-Africa trade is $72 bn against $200 bn for China-Africa. Manmohan Singh saw no real rivalry, and India should rely on its own strengths in IT, pharmaceuticals and capacity building rather than imitate China.

flashcards.front: Why is Latin America turning towards India, and what is the 2010 IDB report?
flashcards.back: The Inter-American Development Bank report 'India: Latin America's next big thing' (2010) shows the region looking to India. There is resentment of China for non-eco-friendly practices, high returns, not using local manpower and land grabbing.

flashcards.front: What steps have institutionalised India-Latin America ties, and how does trade compare with China?
flashcards.back: CELAC held its outreach summit in New Delhi in 2012, a programme of action and a special office followed, and India became an observer in the Pacific Alliance. Trade reached $100 bn in 2017 against China's $264 bn.

answers.question: Examine the evolution of India-Africa relations and the challenges the partnership faces today.
answers.intro: India and Africa share history, geography and a demographic dividend. Relations moved from active support for liberation, through neglect in the 1970s to 90s, to renewed engagement, and today face challenges of Chinese competition, policy gaps and social friction.
body: Evolution: Gandhi wanted a commerce of ideas and services, not raw materials, and Nehru saw India's independence as incomplete without Africa's liberation. India backed liberation till the 1960s, then neglected Africa after African attitudes to the 1962 war and attacks on the diaspora.

Revival: since the 1990s Indian IT and pharmaceutical firms led engagement, and government followed late with the first India-Africa summit in 2008, eight years after China; the 2015 summit drew all 54 countries, supported by ITEC, Team 9 and the Pan-African e-network.

Challenges: China's trade with Africa is $200 bn against India's $72 bn; India has no declared Africa policy, limited diplomatic presence and diaspora reach confined to the elite; some Indian companies face resentment over land grabbing.

Way forward: draw redlines and enforce CSR for private firms, create special purpose vehicles for fast delivery, follow Mahesh Sachdev's SWOT approach with African stakeholders, address racial violence against Africans in India, and promote African studies.
answers.conclusion: India's partnership with Africa works best as a genuine two-way street built on capacity building rather than extraction. A declared Africa policy bringing government, private sector and diaspora together would give the Gandhian vision of ideas and services credible shape.

answers.question: Latin America is the last frontier of India's foreign policy. Discuss the opportunities and constraints in India-Latin America relations.
answers.intro: Latin America remains the last frontier of India's foreign policy, held back more by psychology than geography. The notes show rising opportunity as the region looks to India, set against China's far larger presence and India's connectivity gaps.
body: Past neglect: India met Latin America mainly at the UN General Assembly or NAM, with Cuba the exception, because the region faced instability and heavy US domination and India's economy was inward looking.

Opportunity: after the Cold War stability and growth arrived, and Indian IT, pharmaceutical, oil and gas and edible oil firms led trade. The 2010 IDB report 'India: Latin America's next big thing' reflects resentment of China's land grabbing and neglect of local manpower.

Market logic: a 600 mn population with per capita income of $11,000 and reserves of oil, gas and minerals; yet India lacks direct flights and consulates in all countries, and holds PTAs only with Chile and Mercosur, so FTAs and shipping incentives are needed.

Institutionalisation: CELAC held its outreach summit in New Delhi in 2012, a programme of action and a special coordinating office followed, and India gained Pacific Alliance observer status; trade reached $100 bn in 2017, against China's $264 bn.
scholars: IDB report: India, Latin America's next big thing (2010)
answers.conclusion: India's late start in Latin America need not be fatal, since the region is itself looking to India. Better connectivity, trade agreements, frequent high-level visits and mutual area studies would turn the existing private-sector base into a durable partnership.
